question:
The **binding energy of the deuteron** ($^2\!H$) is $BE=2.224\,\text{MeV}$.

Assume (for estimation) that the attractive **nuclear force** between the proton and neutron acts effectively over a range of about $r_0=2.0\,\text{fm}$, and that the average attractive force magnitude can be approximated by
 $F_{n,avg}\approx \frac{BE}{r_0}.$ 

Also use the convenient Coulomb constant in nuclear units:

 $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}e^2 \approx 1.44\,\text{MeV\,fm}$, 

so that the magnitude of Coulomb repulsive force between two protons at separation $r$ is
 $F_C\approx \frac{1.44}{r^2}\;\text{MeV/fm}.$ 

(Useful conversions: $1\,\text{MeV}=1.602\times10^{-13}\,\text{J}$, $1\,\text{fm}=10^{-15}\,\text{m}$.)

A student claims: “At separations of the order of a few femtometres, Coulomb repulsion must dominate, so a bound nucleus like deuteron cannot exist.”

(a) Estimate $F_{n,avg}$ in MeV/fm and in newtons.</br>
(b) Estimate $F_C$ at $r=2.0\,\text{fm}$ (in MeV/fm and in newtons) for a hypothetical proton–proton pair at the same separation.</br>
(c) Using (a) and (b), **evaluate** the student’s claim and conclude which interaction dominates at $\sim 2\,\text{fm}$ and why the existence of bound nuclei supports the short-range but strong nature of nuclear force.</br>

options.A: $F_{n,avg}\approx 1.11\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 178\,\text{N}$ and $F_C(2\,\text{fm})\approx 0.36\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 58\,\text{N}$; nuclear attraction dominates, so the claim is incorrect
options.B: $F_{n,avg}\approx 0.11\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 18\,\text{N}$ and $F_C(2\,\text{fm})\approx 0.36\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 58\,\text{N}$; Coulomb dominates, so the claim is correct
options.C: $F_{n,avg}\approx 1.11\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 178\,\text{N}$ and $F_C(2\,\text{fm})\approx 3.6\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 576\,\text{N}$; Coulomb dominates, so the claim is correct
options.D: $F_{n,avg}\approx 11.1\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 1780\,\text{N}$ and $F_C(2\,\text{fm})\approx 0.036\,\text{MeV/fm}\approx 5.8\,\text{N}$; nuclear attraction dominates but this contradicts mass–energy equivalence
